title: Rarest CarsUpdated Jul 06, 202610 Rarest Cars in the World

contentBlocks.text: Driving a new Lamborghini or a custom Porsche will definitely get you noticed. It feels good to have people look, but owning a car like that mostly just shows you have money. If you earn enough from a successful business or get a big inheritance, you can just go out and buy one.

The cars on this list are different. You cannot just walk into a dealership and buy them, no matter how much money you have. We are not talking about those modern limited editions that car companies make just to charge more, either. True rarity usually happens by accident. Many of these cars are the only ones left because others were lost in wars, destroyed in factory fires, or ruined in tough races.

To most people, these might just look like very expensive old cars. But they come from an era when people designed cars with pencils and built them by hand, instead of using computer software and wind tunnels.

When one of these cars actually goes up for auction, regular pricing rules do not apply. Bidding doesn't just go up by small amounts; it can jump by millions of dollars in a single moment. Here are ten of the rarest cars in the world, from famous classics to the hardest ones to find.
1. Mercedes-Benz 300 SLR Uhlenhaut Coupé (Only 2)
2. Bugatti Type 57SC Atlantic (Only 4)
3. Aston Martin DBR1 (Only 5)
4. McLaren F1 LM (Only 5)
5. Bugatti Type 41 Royale (Only 6)
6. Jaguar XKSS (Only 16)
7. Alfa Romeo 33 Stradale (Only 18)
8. Aston Martin DB4 GT Zagato (Only 19)
9. Ferrari 250 Testa Rossa (Only 33)
10. Ferrari 250 GTO (Only 36)
1Mercedes-Benz 300 SLR Uhlenhaut Coupé
Only 2

If you want to talk about the absolute king of the classic car world, this is it. Forget every auction record you’ve ever heard of; this Mercedes didn't just break the record in 2022—it completely vaporized it. An anonymous buyer shelled out a staggering 142 million dollars for one of these. To put that into perspective, you could buy a fleet of brand-new private jets or a couple of superyachts for that money, and you’d still have pocket change left over.
So, why is this silver gullwing worth more than a Renaissance masterpiece?

First off, they only made two. Ever. It was designed by Mercedes’ legendary motorsport chief, Rudolf Uhlenhaut, who basically took the company’s absolute weapon of a Formula 1 car and gave it a roof and a license plate. It was supposed to dominate the racing world in 1956, but after a tragic crash at Le Mans in 1955, Mercedes pulled out of racing entirely. The project was canceled, and the race cars were locked away.

But Rudolf wasn't just going to let his masterpiece sit in a dark basement. He ended up using one of the two cars as his personal daily driver. Imagine commuting to work in the 1950s in a straight-eight, 300-horsepower street-legal F1 car that could hit 180 mph. It was so ridiculously loud that Rudolf allegedly had to wear earplugs just to drive it to the office, and rumors say he once made a two-and-a-half-hour trip across Germany in just over an hour because he was late for a meeting.

For over half a century, Mercedes swore they would never, ever sell either of them. They kept both under heavy guard in their museum vaults in Stuttgart. But in May 2022, they secretly invited a tiny handful of the world’s richest collectors to a private auction, unlocked the vault, and parted with one. The other one is still owned by Mercedes and will never leave their sight.

So yeah, unless you have nine figures to throw around and a direct line to the board of directors in Stuttgart, you have a better chance of buying the moon than owning this car. It is the definition of a mechanical unicorn.
2Bugatti Type 57SC Atlantic
Only 4

While we talked about the Mercedes as a great piece of engineering, the Bugatti Type 57SC Atlantic is really in a league of its own when it comes to design. Back in the 1930s, Jean Bugatti wanted to create something faster and better looking than anything else on the road. He only built four of them, and we only know where three of those are today.

These cars are worth over 100 million dollars now, mostly because they look so unique. The most recognizable feature is the raised seam that runs right down the middle of the body. This actually started as a fix for a technical issue. Jean wanted to use a lightweight magnesium-aluminum alloy, but that metal would catch fire if you tried to weld it. To get around that, the team had to rivet the panels together from the outside, which left that famous fin. Even when they started using normal aluminum for the other cars, they kept the seam because it looked so good.

Each of the four cars has its own history. Ralph Lauren owns one, and he had it restored to basically perfect condition. Another one was actually hit by a train in the 1950s. It was eventually rebuilt from the wreck, but collectors still argue about how much of that car is actually original.

The real mystery is the second car, which was Jean Bugatti’s personal prototype known as La Voiture Noire. He drove it every day until 1940. When the German army invaded France during World War II, the factory tried to ship the car to Bordeaux by train to keep it safe. The train made it to the station, but the car was missing.

Nobody knows what happened to it. Was it stolen by a general? Is it just sitting in a garage somewhere in France? If that car ever turned up, it would probably be worth at least 150 million dollars. It is easily the biggest mystery in the car world.
3Aston Martin DBR1
Only 5

While Ferrari was busy dominating world sports car racing in the late 1950s, a small British team was working in the shadows, obsessed with a single goal: beating Enzo Ferrari at his own game. That team was Aston Martin, and the weapon they built was the DBR1. They only made five of them, and this car didn’t just save the company’s reputation—it cemented it in racing history.

To understand why the DBR1 is such a big deal, you have to realize that it wasn’t just a fast road car modified for the track. It was built from scratch purely to win the grueling 24 Hours of Le Mans. Underneath that gorgeous, flowing green aluminum body was a brutally stiff spaceframe chassis and a 3.0-liter straight-six engine. It wasn't the most powerful car on the grid, but it was incredibly agile and reliable.

The payoff came in 1959. Driven by legendary racing icons Carroll Shelby (the mastermind who would later create the Shelby Cobra) and Roy Salvadori, the DBR1 crossed the finish line at Le Mans in first place, giving Aston Martin its first—and only—outright victory at the legendary race.

Because Aston Martin only built five of these machines, they almost never change hands. Most of them are locked away in private collections where money doesn’t matter. But back in 2017, chassis number one—the very first DBR1 built—headed to the RM Sotheby’s auction at Pebble Beach. When the hammer fell, it sold for a mind-boggling 22.5 million dollars. At the time, that single sale made it the most expensive British car ever sold at public auction.

Owning a DBR1 isn’t just about owning a rare piece of metal. It’s about owning the exact moment British engineering finally pushed Ferrari off the top of the podium. If you want a piece of pure, unfiltered motorsport royalty, this is as good as it gets.
4McLaren F1 LM
Only 5

The McLaren F1 LM is one of the rarest cars in existence, with only five ever produced for customers. If you were a car fan in the 1990s, the standard McLaren F1 was already considered the ultimate supercar because of its three-seat layout and gold-lined engine bay. However, after McLaren entered Le Mans in 1995 and took four of the top five spots, they decided to build the LM to celebrate that victory.

The LM was essentially a street-legal version of the Le Mans race car. It was actually more powerful than the racing version because it didn't have to follow track restrictions. While the standard F1 had 618 horsepower, the LM version produced 671 horsepower from its BMW V12 and was significantly lighter.

You can recognize an LM by its Papaya Orange paint, which was the racing color used by the company’s founder, and the large carbon fiber wing on the back. The interior has no luxury features or soundproofing. It is so loud inside that the car came with a built-in intercom system just so the people inside could talk to each other over the engine noise.

Because only five were made, they are almost never seen. The Sultan of Brunei reportedly bought three of them, leaving only two others for the rest of the world. If one were to be sold today, the price would likely start at over 25 million dollars. It remains the most iconic version of what many consider the greatest supercar of the 90s.
5Bugatti Type 41 Royale
Only 6

The Bugatti Type 41 Royale is one of the rarest cars ever made, with only six in existence. Ettore Bugatti originally designed it to outshine every other luxury brand, specifically targeting royalty as his customers. However, the car was released right at the start of the Great Depression, and even kings couldn't justify the cost. Ironically, Bugatti never actually sold a single Royale to a reigning monarch.

The car is massive by any standard. At over 21 feet long and weighing more than three tons, it is larger than most modern pickup trucks. Its 12.7-liter straight-eight engine was originally meant for airplanes. Since Bugatti couldn't sell many of the cars, he ended up using the extra engines he had already built to power trains for the French national railway.

Every Royale was treated as a piece of art. Ettore’s brother, Rembrandt Bugatti, designed the famous radiator cap, which is a small sculpture of an elephant standing on its hind legs. Because different coachbuilders designed the bodies for each chassis, all six cars have a distinct look.

Their survival is also a notable story. During World War II, the Bugatti family hid three of the cars behind a fake wall in their house to keep the German army from taking or destroying them. All six survived the war intact.

Today, these cars are considered museum pieces rather than just vehicles. Most are kept in permanent collections, such as the National Automobile Museum in France. They rarely ever go up for sale, but when they do, they sell for tens of millions of dollars. The Royale stands as a symbol of a time when luxury was defined by extreme scale and ambition.
6Jaguar XKSS
Only 16

The Jaguar XKSS is often called the first supercar, but it was never actually planned that way. In the mid-1950s, Jaguar was very successful at the 24 Hours of Le Mans with their D-Type race car. When the company decided to stop racing after the 1956 season, they were left with 25 unfinished chassis sitting in the factory. To make some money back, co-founder Sir William Lyons decided to turn those race cars into something people could drive on the street.

The changes they made were pretty simple. They added a passenger door, a windshield, a basic folding roof, and chrome bumpers to meet road regulations. Even with those additions, it was still a race car at heart. It had a 3.4-liter engine that could reach 150 mph, which was an intense speed for a road car in 1957.

Jaguar intended to finish all 25 cars, but a major fire broke out at their factory in February 1957. The fire destroyed nine of the chassis, leaving only 16 finished cars. Most of these had already been sent to customers in the United States.

The car became even more famous because of Steve McQueen. He bought one in 1958 and was known for driving it fast through the streets of Los Angeles. He reportedly got so many speeding tickets that the local police chief offered a steak dinner to any officer who could actually catch him.

Today, those 16 original cars are some of the most valuable collector items in the world. When one of them goes up for sale, the price usually reaches 15 to 20 million dollars. It is a rare case of a race car that survived a factory fire to become a piece of history.
7Alfa Romeo 33 Stradale
Only 18

Many car designers consider the Alfa Romeo 33 Stradale to be the most beautiful car ever made. Released in 1967, its name literally means road-going in Italian. To create it, Alfa Romeo took their Tipo 33 race car and had designer Franco Scaglione give it a custom aluminum body. They only built 18 of these, making it extremely rare.

The design was unusual for the time. It had butterfly doors that curved up into a glass roof, making the interior feel like an airplane cockpit. The car sat very low to the ground, only 39 inches tall. It used a mid-mounted 2.0-liter V8 engine. While that sounds small, it was a racing motor that could reach 10,000 RPM and push the lightweight car to 160 mph.

When it first came out, the 33 Stradale was one of the most expensive cars you could buy. It cost about 17,000 dollars at a time when a typical new car in the US cost around 3,000 dollars. It was even more expensive than a Lamborghini Miura. Because it was essentially a race car with a massive price tag, Alfa Romeo had a hard time finding buyers, which is why they stopped production after just 18 units.

Out of those 18 chassis, only 8 were actually finished with the factory Scaglione body. The others were kept by the company or sent to design houses like Pininfarina and Bertone to be used for one-off concept cars.

Today, seeing a 33 Stradale in person is very rare. Most of them are kept in European museums or private collections and almost never appear at public auctions. If one were sold today, experts believe it would cost more than 30 million dollars. For many enthusiasts, it represents the high point of Italian car design.
8Aston Martin DB4 GT Zagato
Only 19

In the early 1960s, Aston Martin had a problem. Their DB4 GT was a great sports car, but it was too heavy to keep up with Ferrari’s dominant 250 GT series on the racetrack. To fix this, Aston Martin sent the car to Milan, Italy, and handed it over to the legendary styling house Zagato. A young designer named Ercole Spada stripped away all the heavy British luxury and rebuilt the car from the ground up. The plan was to build 23 of them, but due to low demand at the time, they stopped after just 19.

Zagato’s team made the car lighter, shorter, and much more aerodynamic. They replaced the standard steel panels with an incredibly thin, lightweight aluminum body, and swapped out the glass windows for plastic ones. The design became famous for its aggressive, muscular curves and Zagato’s signature "double-bubble" roof, which gave extra headroom for racing helmets while keeping the car’s profile as low as possible. Under the hood, the 3.7-liter straight-six engine was tuned to put out 314 horsepower, pushing the car past 150 mph.

Despite all the upgrades, the DB4 GT Zagato couldn't quite beat Ferrari on the track, mostly because Ferrari released the legendary 250 GTO shortly after. Since it didn't bring home the racing trophies Aston Martin had hoped for, and because it carried a huge price premium over the standard car, it was a tough sell in 1961.

However, time has completely changed the narrative for this car. What was once seen as an expensive racing project that fell just short of victory is now viewed as one of the most beautiful and desirable collaborations in automotive history. It represents the perfect marriage of British mechanical engineering and raw Italian styling.

Because only 19 original cars were built in the 1960s, they are deeply prized by collectors. When one occasionally appears at high-end auctions like those at Monterey or Pebble Beach, the bidding routinely starts at around 13 to 15 million dollars. It is a car that proves losing on the track in 1961 doesn't stop you from becoming an absolute legend decades later.
9Ferrari 250 Testa Rossa
Only 33

In the late 1950s, sports car racing was a dangerous business, and Enzo Ferrari needed a car that could actually finish a long-distance race without breaking down. This led to the 250 Testa Rossa. The name means red head in Italian, which was just a reference to the bright red paint on the engine's valve covers. Ferrari only built 33 of these cars between 1957 and 1961, and they became some of the most successful endurance racers the company ever made.

The car's design was mostly a response to the technical problems of the time. The most recognizable versions have pontoon front fenders that are separated from the rest of the body. The designer, Sergio Scaglietti, came up with this shape to help with cooling. The car used drum brakes that would lose their stopping power when they got too hot, so he left big gaps behind the wheels to funnel cold air toward them. While this kept the brakes cool, it also made the car lift at high speeds because air would get trapped underneath. Since this made the car hard to drive on fast straightaways, Ferrari eventually switched back to a smoother, more traditional body design.

Mechanically, the car was pretty straightforward. Instead of building a brand-new engine, Ferrari used a reliable version of their 3.0-liter V12. It produced about 300 horsepower, which was more than enough for a car weighing less than 1,800 pounds. Its real strength was how long it could last. It could run at high speeds for 24 hours straight at Le Mans, which helped Ferrari win that race in 1958, 1960, and 1961.

Because there are only 33 of them, these cars are seen as important historical pieces today. Most of them are still around, but they rarely leave the private collections where they are kept. When one does go up for sale, it is a massive event for collectors. An early model sold for over 16 million dollars at an auction years ago, and private deals for the best examples can now go for over 40 million dollars. The car remains a reminder of a time when Ferrari built race cars purely to win, using whatever design worked best to keep them on the track.
10Ferrari 250 GTO
Only 36

If there is a single car that defines the pinnacle of the classic car market, it is the Ferrari 250 GTO. Built between 1962 and 1964, Ferrari only produced 36 of them. The "O" stands for Omologata, which is Italian for "homologated"—meaning Ferrari built these cars strictly to meet racing production rules so they could compete in the FIA's GT class. Today, it is arguably the most valuable and sought-after automobile on the planet.

What makes the 250 GTO fascinating is that it was almost canceled before it even started. In late 1961, a massive walkout occurred at Ferrari after a major argument between Enzo Ferrari and several key engineers. The lead designer of the GTO project walked out the door, leaving the car unfinished. Enzo had to hand the messy prototype over to a young engineer named Mauro Forghieri and coachbuilder Sergio Scaglietti. They essentially rushed to finish the car, using leftovers from the 250 Testa Rossa engine and a modified chassis from the older 250 GT SWB.

Despite being a bit of a mechanical patchwork, the result was flawless. The 3.0-liter V12 produced 300 horsepower, and because the body had been aggressively tested in a wind tunnel—a rare move at the time—it was incredibly aerodynamic. It completely dominated sports car racing, taking the international championship for Ferrari three years in a row from 1962 to 1964.

Back in 1962, a brand-new 250 GTO cost about 18,000 dollars in the United States. But money wasn’t enough to buy one; buyers had to be personally vetted and approved by Enzo Ferrari himself, or his US distributor Luigi Chinetti, just to make sure you were a serious racer and wouldn't ruin the car's reputation.

For decades, the 250 GTO has held the title for some of the most expensive public and private car sales in history. In 2018, a clean, race-proven example sold privately for a rumored 70 million dollars, and public auction prices consistently hover around the 40-to-50-million-dollar range. It is one of the few cars in the world where every single one of the 36 units built is fully accounted for. It represents a rare, unrepeatable moment where a rushed, dramatic racing project ended up becoming the ultimate investment piece.
Conclusion

When you look at this list, it is pretty clear that these cars were not made in small numbers just to create hype or artificial scarcity. Back in the 1950s and 60s, car companies did not build limited runs to help wealthy people park their money. They built five or six cars because that was all they could afford to make, or because a factory fire destroyed the rest. Sometimes, they only made what they needed to meet a specific racing rule before moving on to something else.

The massive prices these cars fetch today are really about that history. They come from a rough and dangerous time for racing, when cars were built by hand, tested on open roads, and driven to the limit by people who took huge risks. You can build a modern car today with thousands of horsepower and a limited production count, but you can never manufacture the decades of history and racing pedigree that these original cars have in them.

In the end, these cars are more than just vehicles or investments. They are like pieces of history that you can still drive. They serve as a reminder of a very specific time that will not happen again, when a small group of engineers could draw up a design, build a few cars in a workshop, and end up creating a legend that lasts forever.
